about: Thermodynamics 1 (CENG40005) is a core 5-credit module running across the Autumn and Spring terms of Year 1 on Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering, according to the 2026-27 programme specification. No published syllabus for it could be found; the programme specification says module details are in the department's Module Handbook. The topics here are therefore a standard first course in chemical engineering thermodynamics built from the module's title and programme: PVT behaviour and equations of state, the first law for closed and flow systems, heat effects, the second law and entropy, power and refrigeration cycles, and the property relations that lead into phase equilibrium. Check them against your own module handbook. No module-specific assessment breakdown was found; the programme specification gives only a Year 1 average of roughly 70% examination, 20% coursework and 10% practical.
topics: Fundamental concepts, state and the phase rule
PVT behaviour of pure fluids and equations of state
The first law for closed systems
Energy balances for open, steady-flow systems
Heat effects: sensible heat, latent heat and heats of reaction
Property relations and phase equilibrium of pure substances

notes.h: System, state and equilibrium in chemical engineering
notes.body:
Chemical engineering thermodynamics asks two practical questions. How much energy does a process need or release? And what state (phase, composition) will a system reach at equilibrium? Both depend on careful definitions.

Systems and surroundings
- A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings, for example a batch reactor with its valves shut.
- An open system has streams flowing in and out, such as a continuous heat exchanger, compressor, distillation column or reactor.
- An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter.

Properties and state
- Extensive properties depend on how much material there is: total volume V^t, total internal energy U^t and total enthalpy H^t.
- Intensive properties do not: temperature T, pressure P, density, and molar or specific properties such as molar volume V = V^t/n.
- Chemical engineers usually work on a molar basis (J/mol, m³/mol), but steam tables are on a mass basis (kJ/kg). Convert with the molar mass.
- State functions (U, H, S, G, V) depend only on the current state. Heat Q and work W depend on the path.

Equilibrium
- Thermal equilibrium means no temperature differences. Mechanical equilibrium means no unbalanced forces (pressure differences). Phase and chemical equilibrium mean no net tendency for matter to move between phases or to react.
- The zeroth law (two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in thermal equilibrium with each other) makes temperature a measurable property.
- Thermodynamics describes equilibrium states. Rates (kinetics and transfer processes) are dealt with elsewhere in the degree.

Units
- Use SI throughout: Pa (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa), K, J and mol.
- The gas constant is R = 8.314 J/(mol K) = 8.314 Pa m³/(mol K) = 83.14 cm³ bar/(mol K).

The Gibbs phase rule (non-reacting systems)
- F = 2 − π + N, where F is the number of degrees of freedom (independent intensive variables), π is the number of phases and N is the number of chemical species.
- Pure water as a single phase: F = 2 − 1 + 1 = 2, so both T and P can be set independently.
- Boiling water (liquid and vapour): F = 1. Fix P and the boiling temperature is fixed, which is why saturation tables need only one entry.
- The triple point (solid, liquid and vapour): F = 0. It occurs at one fixed T and P, about 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa for water.
- The phase rule fixes only intensive state. The relative amounts of each phase (for example the quality of wet steam) are extensive and need an extra balance.

Worked example: 1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K and 1 bar has V = RT/P = 8.314 × 300/10⁵ ≈ 0.0249 m³, or about 24.9 L.

Exam tips: state clearly whether your system is open or closed, and whether you are working per mole, per kg or for the whole system. Many lost marks come from mixing molar and mass units or from using °C in RT.

notes.h: Real-gas behaviour, compressibility and cubic equations of state
notes.body:
Process design needs to know how volume depends on temperature and pressure for gases and liquids. The ideal-gas law is only a starting point. At high pressures or near condensation, real fluids depart from it significantly.

The PT and PV diagrams of a pure substance
- On a PT diagram, the sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet at the triple point. The vaporisation curve ends at the critical point (T_c, P_c).
- On a PV diagram, isotherms below T_c show a horizontal two-phase section under the saturation dome. The critical isotherm has a horizontal point of inflection at the critical point: (∂P/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0.
- Above T_c, the substance cannot be liquefied by compression alone. For water, T_c ≈ 647.1 K and P_c ≈ 220.6 bar. For CO₂, T_c ≈ 304.2 K and P_c ≈ 73.8 bar.

Compressibility factor
- Z = PV/(RT), which equals 1 for an ideal gas. Z < 1 usually means attractive forces dominate. Z > 1 at high pressure means the finite size of the molecules dominates.
- Corresponding states: fluids at the same reduced temperature T_r = T/T_c and reduced pressure P_r = P/P_c have similar Z. Generalised charts and correlations use this idea, with the acentric factor ω as a third parameter in more accurate versions.

Virial equation
- Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + …, or, truncated after the second term, Z = 1 + BP/(RT).
- B and C depend on temperature only, for a given gas. The two-term form works for gases at low to moderate pressure.
- Example: with B = −1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol at 300 K and 10 bar, Z = 1 − (1.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 10⁶)/(8.314 × 300) ≈ 0.940. The molar volume is about 6% below the ideal-gas value.

Cubic equations of state
- Van der Waals: P = RT/(V − b) − a/V². The constant b allows for the volume of the molecules, and a/V² for the attraction between them.
- Fitting to the critical point gives a = 27R²T_c²/(64P_c) and b = RT_c/(8P_c).
- Later cubics (Redlich–Kwong, Soave–Redlich–Kwong, Peng–Robinson) have the same structure but more accurate temperature dependence. They are widely used in process simulators.
- Below T_c a cubic can give three real roots for V. The largest is the vapour volume, the smallest is the liquid volume, and the middle root has no physical meaning.

Worked example: 1 mol of CO₂ in 0.5 L at 300 K, with van der Waals constants from the critical point: a ≈ 0.366 Pa m⁶/mol² and b ≈ 4.28 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol.
- Ideal gas: P = RT/V ≈ 49.9 bar.
- Van der Waals: P = 8.314 × 300/(5 × 10⁻⁴ − 4.28 × 10⁻⁵) − 0.366/(5 × 10⁻⁴)² ≈ 54.6 − 14.6 ≈ 39.9 bar, so Z ≈ 0.80.
- The ideal-gas law overestimates the pressure by about 25% here.

Liquids
- Liquid volumes change little with pressure. They are often treated as incompressible, or estimated with correlations such as Rackett's.

Exam tips: give the units of a and b, set out each term of a cubic separately, and say which root you take. When asked whether a gas is ideal, calculate Z or the reduced conditions; don't just assert it.

notes.h: Internal energy, enthalpy, work and heat in closed systems
notes.body:
The first law of thermodynamics says energy is conserved. For a closed system with negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy, ΔU^t = Q + W.

Sign convention
- Many chemical engineering texts take W as work done on the system and Q as heat added to the system, both positive. That gives ΔU = Q + W.
- Mechanical engineering texts often use W done by the system, which gives ΔU = Q − W.
- Use your lecture-note convention and state it in every answer.

Work
- Reversible expansion or compression work on the system: W = −∫P dV^t.
- Constant volume: W = 0, so Q = ΔU.
- Constant pressure (reversible, PV work only): W = −PΔV^t, so Q = ΔU + PΔV = ΔH.
- This is why enthalpy, H = U + PV, is so useful: at constant pressure, heat equals the enthalpy change.

Heat capacities
- C_V = (∂U/∂T)_V and C_P = (∂H/∂T)_P.
- For an ideal gas, U and H depend on T only, so ΔU = ∫C_V dT and ΔH = ∫C_P dT for any process. Also C_P − C_V = R (molar).
- Monatomic ideal gas: C_V = (3/2)R and C_P = (5/2)R. Diatomic near room temperature: C_V ≈ (5/2)R and C_P ≈ (7/2)R.
- Over wide temperature ranges, C_P is usually given as a polynomial in T, such as C_P/R = A + BT + CT² + DT⁻², and integrated.

Ideal-gas processes (n mol, reversible, work on gas)
- Isothermal: ΔU = 0 and W = −Q = nRT ln(P₂/P₁). Expansion (P₂ < P₁) gives W < 0: the gas does work.
- Isobaric: Q = ΔH = nC_PΔT and W = −nRΔT.
- Isochoric: Q = ΔU = nC_VΔT and W = 0.
- Adiabatic with constant heat capacities: Q = 0, W = ΔU = nC_VΔT, T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^(R/C_P) and PV^γ = constant.

Worked example: 2 mol of a diatomic ideal gas at 300 K expands from 10 bar to 1 bar.
- Isothermal and reversible: W = 2 × 8.314 × 300 × ln(0.1) ≈ −11.5 kJ. The gas does 11.5 kJ of work and absorbs 11.5 kJ of heat.
- Isothermal but against a constant external pressure of 1 bar (irreversible): the work done by the gas is P_ext(V₂ − V₁) = nRT(1 − P₂/P₁) ≈ 4.49 kJ. This is less than the reversible value, which is the most work an expansion can deliver.
- Adiabatic and reversible: T₂ = 300 × 0.1^(2/7) ≈ 155 K, and the work done by the gas is nC_V(T₁ − T₂) ≈ 6.0 kJ.

Exam tips: write the first law with your sign convention, decide whether the process is reversible before using ∫P dV, and remember that ΔU and ΔH depend only on the end states, while Q and W depend on the path.

notes.h: The first law for flow processes and process equipment
notes.body:
Most chemical plants run continuously, so the energy balance is usually applied to open systems in steady state. This topic links directly to the energy balances in Process Analysis.

General energy balance for a control volume
- Rate of accumulation = Σ(in) − Σ(out) of [H + u²/2 + zg] ṁ, + Q̇ + Ẇ_s.
- Here u is velocity, Q̇ is the heat added and Ẇ_s is shaft work done on the fluid (chemical engineering convention).
- Enthalpy appears instead of internal energy because each stream carries its internal energy plus the flow work PV needed to push it across the boundary.

Steady state, one inlet and one outlet
- Δ[H + u²/2 + zg] ṁ = Q̇ + Ẇ_s.
- In most process equipment the kinetic and potential energy terms are tiny compared with ΔH, so ṁΔH = Q̇ + Ẇ_s.
- Check this in nozzles and in high-velocity or tall systems, where it may not hold.

Standard equipment
- Heat exchanger, heater or cooler: no shaft work, so Q̇ = ṁΔH. For a liquid with constant c_P, Q̇ = ṁc_PΔT. For a two-stream exchanger with no heat loss, the heat lost by the hot stream equals the heat gained by the cold one.
- Pump: Ẇ_s = ṁΔH. For an incompressible liquid with negligible temperature rise, the reversible work is VΔP per unit mass or mole.
- Compressor (adiabatic): Ẇ_s = ṁΔH. For an ideal gas with constant C_P, Ẇ_s = ṅC_P(T₂ − T₁).
- Turbine or expander (adiabatic): the shaft work done on the fluid is negative, and the power produced is ṁ(H₁ − H₂).
- Throttle or valve (adiabatic, no work, small Δu): H₂ = H₁. For an ideal gas the temperature is unchanged. Real gases usually cool (the Joule–Thomson effect), which is the basis of many liquefaction processes.
- Mixer: Σ ṁ_in H_in = Σ ṁ_out H_out when adiabatic.

Choosing a reference state
- Only enthalpy differences matter. Choose a reference state, for example the components at 25 °C, or the steam-table reference (saturated liquid water at the triple point), and use it consistently for every stream.

Worked example 1 (heater): 2 kg/s of water is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C (c_P ≈ 4.18 kJ/(kg K)).
- Q̇ = 2 × 4.18 × 60 ≈ 502 kW.

Worked example 2 (mixer): 1 kg/s of water at 80 °C mixes adiabatically with 3 kg/s at 20 °C. With constant c_P:
- 1 × 80 + 3 × 20 = 4 × T_out, so T_out = 35 °C.

Worked example 3 (compressor): 1 mol/s of an ideal diatomic gas is compressed adiabatically from 300 K to 450 K.
- Ẇ_s = 1 × 3.5 × 8.314 × 150 ≈ 4.36 kW done on the gas.

Unsteady problems such as filling or emptying a tank keep the accumulation term. Write the mass and energy balances together and integrate them over time.

Exam tips: draw a block diagram with every stream labelled (flow, T, P, phase), state each assumption (steady, adiabatic, negligible kinetic and potential energy), and use one reference state for all enthalpies.

notes.h: Sensible heat, latent heat and standard heats of reaction
notes.body:
Much of a process plant's energy bill comes from three heat effects: changing temperature (sensible heat), changing phase (latent heat) and carrying out reactions (heat of reaction). Energy balances on real processes combine all three.

Sensible heat
- With no phase change or reaction, at constant pressure: ΔH = ∫C_P dT.
- With constant C_P this is C_PΔT. With a polynomial C_P(T), integrate term by term.
- A mean heat capacity ⟨C_P⟩_H, defined as ΔH/ΔT, can be tabulated to save repeated integration.

Latent heat
- A phase change of a pure substance at constant T and P absorbs or releases ΔH_vap (vaporisation), ΔH_fus (fusion) or ΔH_sub (sublimation).
- For water at 100 °C, ΔH_vap ≈ 2257 kJ/kg ≈ 40.7 kJ/mol.
- Trouton's rule: ΔH_n/T_n ≈ 85–88 J/(mol K) for many non-polar liquids at their normal boiling point. Hydrogen-bonded liquids such as water (about 109 J/(mol K)) are well above this range.
- ΔH_vap falls as temperature rises and becomes zero at the critical point. Watson's correlation is a common way to estimate it at other temperatures.

Standard heats of reaction
- ΔH°_r is the enthalpy change when the reaction proceeds as written, with reactants and products each in their standard state (pure, 1 bar, the stated phase) at temperature T, usually 298.15 K.
- The standard heat of formation ΔH°_f is the value for forming 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states. It is zero for elements in their standard states, such as O₂(g) and C(graphite).
- Hess's law: ΔH°_r = Σ ν_i ΔH°_f,i, with ν positive for products and negative for reactants.
- Standard heat of combustion: the reaction with O₂ to give CO₂ and H₂O. Always state whether the water is liquid (gross, or higher, heating value) or vapour (net, or lower, heating value).

Worked example: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g), with ΔH°_f values (kJ/mol) of CH₄ −74.5, CO₂ −393.5 and H₂O(g) −241.8.
- ΔH°_r = (−393.5) + 2(−241.8) − (−74.5) = −802.6 kJ/mol.
- With liquid water (ΔH°_f ≈ −285.8 kJ/mol) the result is about −890.6 kJ/mol. The difference is twice the latent heat of water at 25 °C.

Temperature dependence (Kirchhoff)
- ΔH°_r(T) = ΔH°_r(T₀) + ∫ΔC°_P dT, where ΔC°_P = Σ ν_i C°_P,i.

Energy balances on reactors
- Use a path: cool the reactants to 298.15 K, react at 298.15 K, then heat the products to the outlet temperature. Because H is a state function, the path is your choice.
- Q̇ = ΣΔH_sensible + ξ̇ΔH°_r(298), where ξ̇ is the rate of reaction (extent).
- If the reactor is adiabatic, set Q̇ = 0 and solve for the outlet temperature. This gives the adiabatic flame (or reaction) temperature.

Exam tips: write the balanced equation with phases, list ΔH°_f values with signs, multiply by the stoichiometric coefficients, and state whether H₂O is liquid or vapour.

notes.h: The second law, entropy and reversibility
notes.body:
The first law balances energy. The second law tells us which processes can actually happen, gives the maximum work available, and introduces entropy, the property at the heart of later work on equilibrium.

Statements of the second law
- No process can have as its only result the complete conversion of heat absorbed by a system into work (the Kelvin–Planck form).
- No process can have as its only result the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter one (the Clausius form).
- Heat engines therefore always reject some heat, and refrigerators always need work.

Entropy
- For a reversible process, dS^t = dQ_rev/T. Entropy is a state function.
- For any process, ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0. The equality holds only for reversible processes.
- Entropy generation measures irreversibility. Causes include friction, mixing, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion and chemical reaction away from equilibrium.

Entropy changes of ideal gases
- ΔS = ∫C_P dT/T − R ln(P₂/P₁) per mole. With constant C_P: ΔS = C_P ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁).
- Isothermal expansion of n mol from P₁ to P₂: ΔS = nR ln(P₁/P₂).
- Example: 2 mol from 10 bar to 1 bar gives ΔS = 2 × 8.314 × ln 10 ≈ +38.3 J/K. This is the same whether the expansion is reversible or not, because S is a state function. Only the surroundings' entropy change and the entropy generated differ.
- Ideal mixing of ideal gases: ΔS_mix = −R Σ y_i ln y_i per mole of mixture. For 1 mol each of two gases, ΔS = 2R ln 2 ≈ 11.5 J/K.

Liquids, solids and reservoirs
- An incompressible liquid or solid: ΔS = C ln(T₂/T₁).
- A heat reservoir receiving heat Q at constant temperature T_R: ΔS = Q/T_R.

Worked example: 1 kg of water (c_P = 4.18 kJ/(kg K)) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by contact with a reservoir at 100 °C.
- ΔS_water = 4.18 ln(353.15/293.15) ≈ 0.778 kJ/K.
- Q = 4.18 × 60 = 250.8 kJ, so ΔS_reservoir = −250.8/373.15 ≈ −0.672 kJ/K.
- S_gen ≈ 0.106 kJ/K, which is positive as required. Heating through a smaller temperature difference would generate less entropy.

Entropy balance for open systems
- At steady state: Σ(ṁS)_out − Σ(ṁS)_in − ΣQ̇_j/T_σ,j = Ṡ_G ≥ 0, where T_σ,j is the temperature of the surroundings at each point where heat crosses the boundary.
- An adiabatic, reversible flow process is isentropic: S_out = S_in. This is the ideal against which compressors and turbines are judged.
- Isentropic efficiency of a compressor: η = ΔH_S/ΔH. Of a turbine: η = ΔH/ΔH_S.

The third law
- The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero. This lets absolute entropies be tabulated.

Exam tips: always calculate ΔS for both the system and the surroundings, use kelvin, remember that ΔS of the system is path-independent, and check that S_gen ≥ 0 at the end.

notes.h: Heat engines, refrigeration cycles and liquefaction
notes.body:
Chemical plants turn heat into power (steam turbines, combined heat and power) and use power to remove heat (refrigeration for low-temperature separation, liquefied natural gas and air separation). The second law sets the limits on both.

Heat engines
- An engine takes |Q_H| from a hot reservoir, produces net work |W| and rejects |Q_C| to a cold reservoir: |W| = |Q_H| − |Q_C|.
- Thermal efficiency: η = |W|/|Q_H|. For a Carnot (fully reversible) engine, η = 1 − T_C/T_H, the maximum possible.
- The steam power plant (Rankine cycle) is the practical version: pump, boiler, turbine and condenser. Its efficiency is found from steam-table enthalpies: η = (W_turbine − W_pump)/Q_boiler.

Refrigerators and heat pumps
- A refrigerator uses work |W| to remove |Q_C| from a cold space and reject |Q_H| = |Q_C| + |W|.
- Coefficient of performance: ω = |Q_C|/|W|. The Carnot limit is ω = T_C/(T_H − T_C).
- A heat pump's useful output is |Q_H|, so COP_HP = |Q_H|/|W| = ω + 1.
- Example: the best possible refrigerator between −10 °C and 35 °C has ω = 263.15/45 ≈ 5.85.

The vapour-compression cycle
- 1→2: saturated vapour leaving the evaporator is compressed (ideally isentropically) to the condenser pressure.
- 2→3: the vapour is desuperheated and condensed to saturated liquid, rejecting heat.
- 3→4: the liquid is throttled through an expansion valve. This is isenthalpic (H₄ = H₃) and gives a cold, low-quality two-phase mixture.
- 4→1: the mixture evaporates in the evaporator, absorbing heat from the cold space.
- ω = (H₁ − H₄)/(H₂ − H₁), with enthalpies from refrigerant tables or a P–H diagram.
- Example (illustrative data): H₁ = 400, H₂ = 430 and H₃ = H₄ = 250 kJ/kg. The refrigeration effect is 150 kJ/kg, the work is 30 kJ/kg, so ω = 5.0, and the heat rejected is 180 kJ/kg.
- Real cycles fall short of Carnot because of the throttling loss, the compressor's inefficiency and the finite temperature differences needed in the heat exchangers.
- Refrigerant choice balances suitable saturation pressures and temperatures with low toxicity and flammability, and with regulations on ozone depletion and global-warming potential.

Liquefaction
- Gases such as nitrogen, oxygen and methane are liquefied by cooling below their critical temperature.
- In the Linde (Joule–Thomson) process, compressed gas is cooled against returning cold gas and then throttled. Part of it condenses because a real gas below its inversion temperature cools on throttling.
- An energy balance on the cold section gives the fraction liquefied: z = (H₄ − H₁)/(H₄ − H_f), where H₄ is the returning low-pressure gas, H₁ the high-pressure feed and H_f the saturated liquid.
- Replacing the throttle partly with a work-producing expander (the Claude process) cools the gas more and raises the yield.

Exam tips: draw each cycle on a T–S or P–H diagram, label the states, tabulate enthalpies, and keep heat and work as magnitudes with a clear statement of direction. Compare the result with the Carnot limit as a check.

notes.h: Property relations, Gibbs energy and the Clapeyron equation
notes.body:
Many properties cannot be measured directly. Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy have to be calculated from measurable P, V, T and heat-capacity data. The fundamental property relations make this possible, and they also give the conditions for phase equilibrium.

Fundamental property relations (1 mol of a homogeneous, closed system)
- dU = T dS − P dV
- dH = T dS + V dP
- dA = −P dV − S dT, where A = U − TS is the Helmholtz energy.
- dG = V dP − S dT, where G = H − TS is the Gibbs energy.
- These relate properties only, so they hold for any process between equilibrium states, reversible or not.

Maxwell relations
These come from the equality of mixed second derivatives:
- (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂P/∂S)_V
- (∂T/∂P)_S = (∂V/∂S)_P
- (∂P/∂T)_V = (∂S/∂V)_T
- (∂V/∂T)_P = −(∂S/∂P)_T
They let you replace awkward entropy derivatives with measurable PVT derivatives. For example, (∂H/∂P)_T = V − T(∂V/∂T)_P, which is zero for an ideal gas.

Residual properties
- A residual property is the real-fluid value minus the ideal-gas value at the same T and P, such as H^R = H − H^ig.
- It can be found from an equation of state or a generalised correlation, so ideal-gas heat capacities plus residual properties give the real-fluid H and S.

Gibbs energy and phase equilibrium
- G is the natural function of T and P, which are the variables controlled in most processes.
- At fixed T and P, a closed system moves towards lower G, and at equilibrium G is a minimum.
- For two phases α and β of a pure substance in equilibrium at the same T and P, the molar Gibbs energies (chemical potentials) are equal: G^α = G^β.

The Clapeyron equation
- Following the saturation curve, dG^α = dG^β gives dP^sat/dT = ΔH/(TΔV), where ΔH and ΔV are the changes on going from α to β.
- For melting ice, ΔV is negative (ice is less dense than water), so the slope is negative. It is about −135 bar/K, so very large pressures are needed to lower the melting point noticeably.

The Clausius–Clapeyron equation (vapour–liquid)
- Assume V_vapour ≫ V_liquid, an ideal-gas vapour and constant ΔH_vap. Then d ln P^sat/d(1/T) = −ΔH_vap/R.
- Integrated: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
- A plot of ln P^sat against 1/T is therefore close to a straight line. The empirical Antoine equation, ln P^sat = A − B/(T + C), refines it.

Worked example: water, with ΔH_vap ≈ 40.66 kJ/mol and P^sat = 1.013 bar at 373.15 K.
- At 363.15 K: ln(P₂/1.013) = −(40 660/8.314)(1/363.15 − 1/373.15) ≈ −0.361, so P₂ ≈ 0.706 bar.
- Steam tables give about 0.702 bar, so the error is under 1%.

Looking ahead
- For mixtures, equal chemical potentials in each phase lead to Raoult's law for ideal solutions: y_iP = x_iP_i^sat. This underpins the vapour–liquid equilibrium used in Separation Processes.

Exam tips: always state the assumptions behind Clausius–Clapeyron (ideal-gas vapour, negligible liquid volume, constant ΔH_vap), use kelvin, and check the sign of ΔV for solid–liquid transitions.

cards.b: F = 2 − π + N: degrees of freedom = 2 − number of phases + number of species.

cards.f: Degrees of freedom of boiling pure water
cards.b: F = 2 − 2 + 1 = 1: fixing pressure fixes the boiling temperature (and vice versa).
A property whose value depends only on the current state (U, H, S, G, V), so its change depends only on the end states.
An extensive property divided by the number of moles, e.g. V = V^t/n. It is intensive.
R = 8.314 J/(mol K) = 8.314 Pa m³/(mol K) = 83.14 cm³ bar/(mol K).
About 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa, where solid, liquid and vapour coexist with F = 0.

cards.f: What the phase rule does not tell you
cards.b: The relative amounts of each phase. Those are extensive and need a material or energy balance (e.g. steam quality).
Z = PV/(RT). Z = 1 for an ideal gas; Z < 1 when attractions dominate; Z > 1 when molecular size dominates (high P).
P = RT/(V − b) − a/V². b allows for molecular volume, a/V² for intermolecular attraction.

cards.f: Van der Waals constants from the critical point
cards.b: a = 27R²T_c²/(64P_c), b = RT_c/(8P_c), from (∂P/∂V)_T = (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0 at the critical point.
Z = 1 + BP/(RT), with B a function of T only. Suitable for gases at low to moderate pressure.
Fluids at the same reduced temperature T/T_c and reduced pressure P/P_c have approximately the same Z (improved by the acentric factor ω).

cards.f: Roots of a cubic EOS below T_c
cards.b: Largest root = saturated vapour volume; smallest = saturated liquid volume; the middle root has no physical meaning.
ΔU^t = Q + W, with Q = heat added to and W = work done on the system (closed system, negligible ΔKE and ΔPE).
For a reversible constant-pressure process in a closed system with PV work only, Q = ΔH.
C_V = (∂U/∂T)_V, C_P = (∂H/∂T)_P. For an ideal gas, C_P − C_V = R (molar).
W = nRT ln(P₂/P₁) = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁). ΔU = 0, so Q = −W.
T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^(R/C_P), PV^γ = constant, W = nC_V(T₂ − T₁).
C_V ≈ (5/2)R and C_P ≈ (7/2)R near room temperature, so γ ≈ 1.4.

cards.f: Why reversible expansion gives the most work
cards.b: The external pressure is kept infinitesimally below the gas pressure throughout, so the gas pushes against the largest possible opposing force.
Δ[(H + u²/2 + zg)ṁ] = Q̇ + Ẇ_s, with Q̇ = heat added and Ẇ_s = shaft work done on the fluid.
ṁΔH = Q̇ + Ẇ_s when kinetic- and potential-energy changes are negligible.
Adiabatic, no work, so H₂ = H₁. Ideal gases keep their temperature; real gases usually cool (Joule–Thomson effect).
Ẇ_s = ṅC_P(T₂ − T₁) (work done on the gas, constant C_P).
Approximately V ΔP per unit mass (or mole): small because liquid volume is small.

cards.f: Why enthalpy appears in open-system balances
cards.b: Each stream carries internal energy plus the flow work PV needed to push it across the boundary; U + PV = H.
An arbitrary state at which H is set to zero. Only differences matter, so use the same reference for every stream.
ΔH°_r = Σ ν_i ΔH°_f,i (products positive ν, reactants negative ν). Valid because H is a state function.
Enthalpy change to form 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states. Zero for elements in their standard states.
ΔH_vap at the normal boiling point ≈ (85–88 J/(mol K)) × T_n for many non-polar liquids. It underestimates hydrogen-bonded liquids such as water.
ΔH°_r(T) = ΔH°_r(T₀) + ∫ΔC°_P dT from T₀ to T, with ΔC°_P = Σν_iC°_P,i.
Higher (gross) heating value: product water as liquid. Lower (net): water as vapour. They differ by the latent heat of the water formed.
ΔH_vap ≈ 2257 kJ/kg ≈ 40.7 kJ/mol.
The outlet temperature at which the sensible heat of the products absorbs all the heat released by reaction (Q = 0).
dS^t = dQ_rev/T. Entropy is a state function, so ΔS depends only on the end states.
ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0, with equality only for reversible processes.
ΔS = C_P ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁) per mole (constant C_P).
ΔS_mix = −R Σ y_i ln y_i per mole of mixture (always positive). For an equimolar binary, R ln 2 per mole.

cards.f: Entropy change of a heat reservoir
cards.b: ΔS = Q/T_R, with Q the heat received by the reservoir and T_R its constant temperature.
Σ(ṁS)_out − Σ(ṁS)_in − ΣQ̇_j/T_σ,j = Ṡ_G ≥ 0.
The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance is zero at 0 K, so absolute entropies can be tabulated.
η = 1 − T_C/T_H (kelvin): the maximum efficiency of any engine operating between reservoirs at T_H and T_C.
ω = T_C/(T_H − T_C) (kelvin). The heat-pump COP is ω + 1 = T_H/(T_H − T_C).
ω = (H₁ − H₄)/(H₂ − H₁): refrigeration effect ÷ compressor work, with H₄ = H₃ across the expansion valve.

cards.f: Why an expansion valve rather than a turbine?
cards.b: The work recoverable from expanding a liquid is small, and a valve is cheap, simple and reliable. The price is an irreversible, isenthalpic expansion.
z = (H₄ − H₁)/(H₄ − H_f), from an energy balance on the adiabatic exchanger, valve and separator.
A real gas below its inversion temperature cools on isenthalpic throttling. This is the basis of the Linde process.
|Q_H| = |Q_C| + |W|: the condenser rejects the heat removed plus the compressor work.
dG = V dP − S dT (1 mol, closed, homogeneous). So (∂G/∂P)_T = V and (∂G/∂T)_P = −S.
At equilibrium between phases at the same T and P, the molar Gibbs energies (chemical potentials) are equal: G^α = G^β.
dP^sat/dT = ΔH/(TΔV) along a two-phase coexistence curve.
ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Assumes ideal-gas vapour, negligible liquid volume and constant ΔH_vap.
(∂V/∂T)_P = −(∂S/∂P)_T: lets entropy's pressure dependence be found from PVT data.
M^R = M − M^ig at the same T and P: the real-fluid correction to an ideal-gas property, found from an EOS or a correlation.

cards.f: Why the ice–water line slopes backwards
cards.b: On melting, ΔH > 0 but ΔV < 0 (ice is less dense), so dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV) is negative (about −135 bar/K).
y_iP = x_iP_i^sat for an ideal liquid solution in equilibrium with an ideal-gas vapour.

questions.q: Which of these is an extensive property?
options: Total enthalpy of a vessel's contents
questions.why: Total enthalpy doubles if you double the amount of material, so it is extensive. Molar volume is extensive volume divided by moles, which makes it intensive. Temperature and pressure do not depend on the amount of material.

questions.q: How many degrees of freedom does pure water have at its triple point?
questions.why: F = 2 − π + N = 2 − 3 + 1 = 0, so the triple point is a single fixed temperature and pressure. 1 is the answer for two coexisting phases (π = 2), which forgets the solid phase. 2 is the single-phase answer. 4 comes from writing the rule with the signs reversed, 2 + π − N.

questions.q: State the Gibbs phase rule for a non-reacting system and use it to explain why a saturated-steam table needs only one independent variable, whereas a superheated-steam table needs two.
markScheme: F = 2 − π + N, terms defined (1)
Saturated steam: π = 2, N = 1, so F = 1 (1)
So one variable (T or P) fixes all intensive saturated properties (1)
Superheated steam: π = 1, so F = 2; T and P both needed (1)
questions.modelAnswer: For a non-reacting system, F = 2 − π + N, where F is the number of independent intensive variables, π the number of phases and N the number of species. For saturated water and steam in equilibrium, π = 2 and N = 1, so F = 1. Choosing either the pressure or the temperature fixes every intensive property of each saturated phase, so a saturation table can be listed against one variable. For superheated steam there is only one phase, so F = 2, and two variables (usually T and P) are needed to fix the state. That is why superheat tables are two-way tables.

questions.q: Taking a = 0.366 Pa m⁶/mol² and b = 4.28 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, what pressure does the van der Waals equation give for 1 mol of CO₂ in 0.5 L at 300 K?
questions.why: P = RT/(V − b) − a/V² = 54.6 − 14.6 ≈ 39.9 bar. 49.9 bar is the ideal-gas value, RT/V. 54.6 bar keeps the excluded-volume term but leaves out the attraction term a/V². 35.3 bar keeps the attraction term but ignores b, using RT/V − a/V².

questions.q: A gas has second virial coefficient B = −1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol at 300 K. Using Z = 1 + BP/(RT), what is Z at 10 bar?
questions.why: BP/(RT) = (−1.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 10⁶)/(8.314 × 300) ≈ −0.060, so Z ≈ 0.940. Dropping the minus sign on B gives 1.060. Putting P in bar while B is in m³/mol makes the correction about 6 × 10⁻⁷, so Z looks like 1.000. 0.060 is just the size of the correction term, without the leading 1.

questions.q: Starting from the conditions at the critical point, show that the van der Waals constants are a = 27R²T_c²/(64P_c) and b = RT_c/(8P_c). Outline each step.
markScheme: States conditions (∂P/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0 at the critical point (1)
Writes the two derivative equations correctly (1)
Divides them to get V_c = 3b, then a = 27RT_c b/8 (1)
Substitutes into the EOS: P_c = RT_c/(2b) − a/(9b²) = RT_c/(8b), so b = RT_c/(8P_c) (1)
Hence a = 27RT_c b/8 = 27R²T_c²/(64P_c) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: At the critical point the critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection, so (∂P/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)_T = 0. From P = RT/(V − b) − a/V²: (1) −RT_c/(V_c − b)² + 2a/V_c³ = 0 and (2) 2RT_c/(V_c − b)³ − 6a/V_c⁴ = 0. Rearranging, (1) gives RT_c/(V_c − b)² = 2a/V_c³ and (2) gives RT_c/(V_c − b)³ = 3a/V_c⁴. Dividing (2) by (1): 1/(V_c − b) = 3/(2V_c), so V_c = 3b. Putting V_c = 3b into (1): RT_c/(4b²) = 2a/(27b³), so a = 27RT_c b/8. Substituting into the equation of state at the critical point: P_c = RT_c/(2b) − a/(9b²) = RT_c/(2b) − 3RT_c/(8b) = RT_c/(8b), so b = RT_c/(8P_c). Finally a = 27RT_c b/8 = 27RT_c/8 × RT_c/(8P_c) = 27R²T_c²/(64P_c). A by-product is Z_c = P_cV_c/(RT_c) = 3/8 = 0.375, which is larger than the 0.23–0.29 found for most real fluids. That is one reason van der Waals is only qualitative.

questions.q: 2 mol of ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 10 bar to 1 bar. How much work does the gas do?
questions.why: The work done by the gas is nRT ln(P₁/P₂) = 2 × 8.314 × 300 × ln 10 ≈ 11.5 kJ. 4.49 kJ is the work for an irreversible expansion against a constant 1 bar, which is a different process. 4.99 kJ comes from using log₁₀ instead of the natural log. ΔU = 0 for an isothermal ideal gas means Q = −W, not that W = 0.

questions.q: 2 mol of a diatomic ideal gas (C_P = 7R/2) expand reversibly and adiabatically from 10 bar and 300 K to 1 bar. What is the final temperature?
questions.why: T₂ = T₁(P₂/P₁)^(R/C_P) = 300 × 0.1^(2/7) ≈ 155 K. 300 K treats the process as isothermal, but in an adiabatic expansion the gas pays for its work from its internal energy, so it cools. 30 K comes from T ∝ P, which holds only at constant volume. About 119 K uses the exponent R/C_V instead of R/C_P.

questions.q: 1 mol of nitrogen (ideal gas, C_P = 7R/2) at 300 K and 1 bar is heated at constant pressure to 500 K, reversibly. Find Q, W, ΔU and ΔH, stating your sign convention.
markScheme: Convention stated: ΔU = Q + W, W = work done on gas (1)
W = −PΔV = −RΔT ≈ −1.66 kJ (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Convention: ΔU = Q + W, with W the work done on the gas. At constant pressure, Q = ΔH = C_PΔT = 3.5 × 8.314 × 200 ≈ 5820 J = 5.82 kJ. ΔU = C_VΔT = 2.5 × 8.314 × 200 ≈ 4157 J ≈ 4.16 kJ. Work on the gas: W = −PΔV = −RΔT = −8.314 × 200 ≈ −1.66 kJ. The gas expands and does 1.66 kJ of work on the surroundings. Check: Q + W = 5.82 − 1.66 = 4.16 kJ = ΔU.

questions.q: A heater raises 2 kg/s of water (c_P = 4.18 kJ/(kg K)) from 20 °C to 80 °C. What is the heat duty?
questions.why: Q̇ = ṁc_PΔT = 2 × 4.18 × 60 ≈ 502 kW. 8.36 kW is ṁc_P alone, which leaves out the temperature rise. 669 kW uses the outlet temperature (80) instead of the 60 K rise. 251 kW is the heat needed per kg/s, which forgets to multiply by the 2 kg/s flow.

questions.q: For an adiabatic steady-flow compressor with negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy, the shaft work per unit mass equals which quantity?
options: The change in specific enthalpy, ΔH
The change in specific internal energy, ΔU
questions.why: With Q̇ = 0 and negligible kinetic and potential energy terms, the steady-flow balance gives Ẇ_s = ṁΔH. Using ΔU leaves out the flow work PV that the fluid carries in and out. −∫P dV is the work for a closed system, not the shaft work of a flow device; for reversible flow the shaft work is ∫V dP. TΔS is the reversible heat, and it is zero here for a reversible adiabatic compressor.

questions.q: 1 kg/s of water at 80 °C and 3 kg/s at 20 °C enter an adiabatic mixing tank operating at steady state. The mixed stream is then heated to 60 °C. Taking c_P = 4.18 kJ/(kg K) and ignoring kinetic and potential energy, find the mixer outlet temperature and the heater duty.
markScheme: Mass balance: 4 kg/s out (1)
Energy balance with reference 0 °C: 1 × 80 + 3 × 20 = 4T (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Mass balance: the outlet carries 1 + 3 = 4 kg/s. For the adiabatic mixer with no work and constant c_P, taking 0 °C as the reference: 1 × 4.18 × 80 + 3 × 4.18 × 20 = 4 × 4.18 × T, so T = (80 + 60)/4 = 35 °C. Heater: Q̇ = ṁc_PΔT = 4 × 4.18 × (60 − 35) = 418 kW.

questions.q: Given ΔH°_f (kJ/mol): CH₄ −74.5, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(g) −241.8, H₂O(l) −285.8. What is ΔH°_r at 298 K for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g)?
questions.why: ΔH°_r = −393.5 + 2(−241.8) − (−74.5) = −802.6 kJ/mol. −890.6 uses the liquid-water value, but the equation specifies water vapour. −951.6 adds the methane term instead of subtracting it. −560.8 forgets the stoichiometric coefficient of 2 on the water.

questions.q: A non-polar liquid boils at 350 K at 1 atm. Using Trouton's rule with 88 J/(mol K), what is the estimated latent heat of vaporisation?
questions.why: ΔH_vap ≈ 88 × 350 = 30 800 J/mol ≈ 30.8 kJ/mol. 0.25 kJ/mol comes from dividing 88 by 350 instead of multiplying. About 6.8 kJ/mol uses the boiling point in °C (about 76.85). About 2.9 kJ/mol uses R × T, but Trouton's constant is about 10.5R, not R.

questions.q: Methane is burned completely with air in a furnace. The reaction is CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g). Using ΔH°_f (kJ/mol) of CH₄ −74.5, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(g) −241.8 and H₂O(l) −285.8, find the standard heat of reaction and the higher heating value per mol of methane. Explain the difference, and outline how you would find the heat released if the products leave at 600 K.
markScheme: Hess's law set up with stoichiometric coefficients (1)
ΔH°_r = −802.6 kJ/mol (lower heating value 802.6 kJ/mol) (1)
With liquid water: −890.6 kJ/mol, so HHV ≈ 890.6 kJ/mol (1)
Difference = 2 × (285.8 − 241.8) = 88 kJ/mol = latent heat of the 2 mol water (1)
Path: react at 298.15 K, then heat the products 298.15 → 600 K with ∫C_P dT for each product (incl. N₂ and excess O₂) (1)
Q = ξΔH°_r + Σ n_i∫C_P,i dT (negative, heat released) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: By Hess's law, ΔH°_r = (−393.5) + 2(−241.8) − (−74.5) = −802.6 kJ/mol of CH₄, so the lower heating value is 802.6 kJ/mol. If the water is condensed to liquid, ΔH°_r = −393.5 + 2(−285.8) + 74.5 = −890.6 kJ/mol, giving a higher heating value of 890.6 kJ/mol. The 88 kJ/mol difference is the latent heat released when the 2 mol of water vapour condense at 25 °C (2 × 44.0 kJ/mol). For products leaving at 600 K, choose the path: react at 298.15 K, then heat all the products (CO₂, H₂O(g), N₂ and any excess O₂) from 298.15 K to 600 K. Then Q = ξΔH°_r(298) + Σ n_i∫C_P,i dT. The result is still negative, but smaller in magnitude than 802.6 kJ per mol of CH₄, because some of the heat stays in the hot flue gas.

questions.q: 2 mol of ideal gas expand isothermally from 10 bar to 1 bar. What is the entropy change of the gas?
options: Zero, because the temperature is constant
questions.why: ΔS = nR ln(P₁/P₂) = 2 × 8.314 × ln 10 ≈ +38.3 J/K. −38.3 J/K uses ln(P₂/P₁) without the minus sign that goes in front of the pressure term. +16.6 J/K uses log₁₀ instead of the natural log. Constant temperature does not mean constant entropy: the gas spreads into a larger volume, so its entropy rises.

questions.q: 1 kg of water (c_P = 4.18 kJ/(kg K)) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C by a reservoir at 100 °C. How much entropy is generated?
questions.why: ΔS_water = 4.18 ln(353.15/293.15) ≈ 0.778 kJ/K. The reservoir supplies 250.8 kJ at 373.15 K, so ΔS_res ≈ −0.672 kJ/K, and S_gen is the sum, about 0.106 kJ/K. 0.778 is the water's change alone, ignoring the reservoir. −0.672 is the reservoir's change alone, and a negative value can never be the entropy generated. 1.45 adds the two magnitudes, ignoring the fact that the reservoir loses entropy.

questions.q: Equal amounts (1 mol each) of nitrogen and oxygen, both ideal gases at 300 K and 1 bar, are allowed to mix at constant T and total P. Calculate the entropy change and explain why the process is irreversible. What minimum work would be needed to separate the mixture again at 300 K?
markScheme: ΔS_mix = −nR Σ y ln y with n = 2, y = 0.5 (1)
No heat or work exchanged with surroundings, so ΔS_surr = 0 and S_gen > 0: irreversible (1)
Minimum separation work = TΔS = 300 × 11.5 ≈ 3.46 kJ (ideal, isothermal) (2)
questions.modelAnswer: For ideal gases, ΔS_mix = −nR Σ y_i ln y_i = −2 × 8.314 × (0.5 ln 0.5 + 0.5 ln 0.5) = 2 × 8.314 × ln 2 ≈ 11.5 J/K. Ideal gases mix with no change in enthalpy, so no heat flows to the surroundings and their entropy is unchanged. The total entropy therefore rises by 11.5 J/K, so the process is irreversible: the gases never unmix on their own. To reverse it at constant T, a separation device must reduce the system's entropy by 11.5 J/K, rejecting heat TΔS to the surroundings. The minimum (reversible) work is W_min = TΔS_mix = 300 × 11.5 ≈ 3.46 kJ. Real separations need far more.

questions.q: What is the maximum coefficient of performance of a refrigerator removing heat at −10 °C and rejecting it at 35 °C?
questions.why: ω_Carnot = T_C/(T_H − T_C) = 263.15/45 ≈ 5.85. 6.85 is T_H/(T_H − T_C), the heat-pump COP, which counts the heat rejected rather than the heat removed. −0.22 comes from using Celsius, −10/45. 0.854 is T_C/T_H, which is not a COP; it equals 1 minus the Carnot engine efficiency.

questions.q: In a vapour-compression cycle, H₁ = 400 kJ/kg (evaporator exit), H₂ = 430 kJ/kg (compressor exit) and H₃ = 250 kJ/kg (condenser exit). What is the COP as a refrigerator?
questions.why: The valve is isenthalpic, so H₄ = 250. ω = (H₁ − H₄)/(H₂ − H₁) = 150/30 = 5.0. 6.0 is (H₂ − H₃)/(H₂ − H₁), the heat-pump COP based on the heat rejected. 13.3 is H₁/(H₂ − H₁), which uses an absolute enthalpy (arbitrary reference) instead of the refrigeration effect H₁ − H₄. 0.20 is the inverse ratio, work ÷ refrigeration.

questions.q: A vapour-compression refrigerator has H₁ = 400 kJ/kg at the evaporator exit, H₂ = 430 kJ/kg at the compressor exit and H₃ = 250 kJ/kg at the condenser exit. It must remove 15 kW from a cold store at −10 °C, rejecting heat at 35 °C. Find the refrigerant flow rate, the compressor power and the condenser duty, and compare the COP with the Carnot value.
markScheme: H₄ = H₃ = 250 kJ/kg (isenthalpic valve) (1)
Compressor power = 0.1 × 30 = 3.0 kW (1)
Condenser duty = 0.1 × 180 = 18 kW (= 15 + 3) (1)
COP = 5.0 vs Carnot ≈ 5.85; shortfall due to throttling loss, compressor irreversibility and finite temperature differences (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Across the expansion valve H₄ = H₃ = 250 kJ/kg, so the refrigeration effect is 400 − 250 = 150 kJ/kg. Flow rate: ṁ = 15/150 = 0.10 kg/s. Compressor power: 0.10 × (430 − 400) = 3.0 kW. Condenser duty: 0.10 × (430 − 250) = 18 kW, which matches the 15 kW removed plus the 3 kW of work. COP = 15/3 = 5.0. The Carnot limit for −10 °C and 35 °C is 263.15/45 ≈ 5.85, so the cycle reaches about 85% of it. The gap comes from the irreversible throttling, the non-ideal compression and desuperheating, and in a real plant the refrigerant must run colder than the store and hotter than the surroundings to drive the heat transfer.

questions.q: Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation with ΔH_vap = 40.66 kJ/mol, and P^sat = 1.013 bar at 373.15 K, estimate the vapour pressure of water at 363.15 K.
questions.why: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(40 660/8.314)(1/363.15 − 1/373.15) ≈ −0.361, giving P₂ ≈ 0.706 bar, close to the tabulated 0.702 bar. Dropping the minus sign gives about 1.45 bar, a higher pressure at a lower temperature, which cannot be right. Using 90 and 100 (°C) in the 1/T terms gives about 0.0044 bar. 0.986 bar scales the pressure in proportion to absolute temperature as if the vapour were a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, ignoring evaporation and condensation.

questions.q: For pure water in equilibrium with its vapour at given T and P, which molar property is the same in both phases?
questions.why: Phase equilibrium at fixed T and P means G is at a minimum, so the molar Gibbs energy is the same in each phase. Enthalpy differs by ΔH_vap, the latent heat. Entropy differs by ΔH_vap/T. Volume differs greatly between liquid and vapour, except at the critical point.

questions.q: Starting from dG = V dP − S dT, derive the Clapeyron equation for two phases α and β of a pure substance in equilibrium. Then state the extra assumptions that give the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
markScheme: Equilibrium: G^α = G^β along the coexistence curve, so dG^α = dG^β (1)
V^α dP − S^α dT = V^β dP − S^β dT, giving dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV (1)
At equilibrium ΔS = ΔH/T (reversible phase change at constant T, P), so dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV) (1)
Assumptions: V_vap ≫ V_liq so ΔV ≈ V_vap; ideal-gas vapour V = RT/P (1)
Gives d ln P/dT = ΔH/(RT²); constant ΔH integrates to ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Along the coexistence curve both phases are at the same T and P and G^α = G^β. Moving along the curve keeps them equal, so dG^α = dG^β. Using dG = V dP − S dT for each phase: V^α dP − S^α dT = V^β dP − S^β dT, so dP^sat/dT = (S^β − S^α)/(V^β − V^α) = ΔS/ΔV. The phase change happens reversibly at constant T and P, so ΔS = ΔH/T, which gives the Clapeyron equation dP^sat/dT = ΔH/(TΔV). For vaporisation far below the critical point, assume (i) the liquid volume is negligible, so ΔV ≈ V^v, and (ii) the vapour is an ideal gas, V^v = RT/P. Then dP/dT = PΔH/(RT²), or d ln P/d(1/T) = −ΔH/R. Assuming (iii) constant ΔH and integrating gives ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

questions.q:
1 mol of a diatomic ideal gas (C_V = 5R/2, C_P = 7R/2) is taken around a cycle of three reversible steps. It starts at state 1: 300 K and 1 bar.
1→2: adiabatic compression to 10 bar.
2→3: cooling at constant pressure (10 bar) back to 300 K.
3→1: isothermal expansion back to 1 bar.
(a) Find T₂. [2]
(b) Tabulate Q, W (work done on the gas), ΔU, ΔH and ΔS for each step. [12]
(c) Find the net work and net heat for the cycle, and check that ΔU and ΔS for the cycle are zero. [3]
(d) Is this cycle a heat engine or a refrigerator/heat pump? Explain using the signs. [3]
markScheme: (c) Net W on gas ≈ 5.80 + 2.32 − 5.74 ≈ +2.38 kJ; net Q ≈ −2.38 kJ; ΣΔU = 0 and ΣΔS = 0 (3)
(d) Net work done on the gas and net heat rejected, so it is a work-consuming cycle (refrigerator/heat pump), not an engine (3)
questions.modelAnswer:
Convention: ΔU = Q + W, with W the work done on the gas. R = 8.314 J/(mol K).

(a) For a reversible adiabatic process, T₂ = T₁(P₂/P₁)^(R/C_P) = 300 × 10^(2/7) ≈ 579.2 K.

(b)
Step 1→2 (adiabatic): Q = 0. ΔU = C_V(T₂ − T₁) = 2.5 × 8.314 × 279.2 ≈ +5.80 kJ, so W = ΔU ≈ +5.80 kJ. ΔH = C_P × 279.2 ≈ +8.12 kJ. ΔS = 0 because the step is reversible and adiabatic.

Step 2→3 (isobaric cooling to 300 K): Q = ΔH = C_P(300 − 579.2) ≈ −8.12 kJ. ΔU = C_V(300 − 579.2) ≈ −5.80 kJ. W = −PΔV = −R(T₃ − T₂) = 8.314 × 279.2 ≈ +2.32 kJ (the gas is compressed as it cools). Check: Q + W = −8.12 + 2.32 = −5.80 kJ = ΔU. ΔS = C_P ln(300/579.2) = 29.10 × (−0.6578) ≈ −19.1 J/K.

Step 3→1 (isothermal at 300 K, 10 bar → 1 bar): ΔU = ΔH = 0. W = RT ln(P₁/P₃) = 8.314 × 300 × ln(0.1) ≈ −5.74 kJ, so the gas does 5.74 kJ of work. Q = −W ≈ +5.74 kJ. ΔS = R ln(P₃/P₁) = 8.314 ln 10 ≈ +19.1 J/K.

(c) Net work on the gas: 5.80 + 2.32 − 5.74 ≈ +2.38 kJ. Net heat: 0 − 8.12 + 5.74 ≈ −2.38 kJ. The two cancel, so ΔU_cycle = 0, as it must for a state function. Also ΣΔU = 5.80 − 5.80 + 0 = 0, ΣΔH = 8.12 − 8.12 + 0 = 0 and ΣΔS = 0 − 19.1 + 19.1 = 0.

(d) Over the cycle there is net work done on the gas (+2.38 kJ) and net heat rejected (−2.38 kJ). The gas absorbs 5.74 kJ at 300 K during the isothermal step and rejects 8.12 kJ during the isobaric step, at temperatures from 579 K down to 300 K. A device that uses net work to take in heat at a low temperature and reject it at a higher one is a refrigerator or heat pump, not a heat engine. As a heat pump its COP would be 8.12/2.38 ≈ 3.4. The value is modest because the heat is delivered over a falling range of temperatures rather than at a single high temperature.

questions.q:
(a) Starting from the condition for equilibrium between two phases of a pure substance, derive the Clapeyron equation. [5]
(b) Hence obtain the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation, stating each assumption. [4]
(c) Water boils at 373.15 K at 1.013 bar, and ΔH_vap = 40.66 kJ/mol. Estimate the vapour pressure at 363.15 K. Comment on the result, given that steam tables give about 0.702 bar. [4]
(d) Steam tables give P^sat ≈ 0.474 bar at 353.15 K and ≈ 1.014 bar at 373.15 K. Use them to estimate an average ΔH_vap over this range, and explain why it differs from 40.66 kJ/mol. [4]
(e) For melting ice at 273.15 K, ΔH_fus ≈ 6.01 kJ/mol and the molar volume falls by about 1.63 cm³/mol. Estimate dP/dT for the melting curve, and explain its sign. [3]
markScheme: (a) G^α = G^β along the curve; dG = V dP − S dT for each phase; dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV = ΔH/(TΔV) (5)
(b) Assumes ΔV ≈ V^v, ideal-gas vapour, constant ΔH: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) (4)
(c) ln(P₂/1.013) ≈ −0.361, so P₂ ≈ 0.706 bar; within about 0.6% of tables (3)
(c) Comment: small error because the temperature range is small and the vapour is nearly ideal at low pressure (1)
(d) Higher than 40.66: ΔH_vap rises as T falls, and the ideal-gas/negligible-liquid assumptions are approximate (2)
(e) dP/dT = 6010/(273.15 × (−1.63 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K ≈ −135 bar/K; negative because ice is less dense than liquid water (3)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Two phases α and β of a pure substance in equilibrium at T and P have equal molar Gibbs energies: G^α(T, P) = G^β(T, P). If T changes by dT and P^sat by dP while both phases remain in equilibrium, then dG^α = dG^β. Using dG = V dP − S dT for each phase: V^α dP − S^α dT = V^β dP − S^β dT, so dP^sat/dT = ΔS/ΔV. The phase change happens reversibly at constant T and P, so ΔS = ΔH/T, which gives dP^sat/dT = ΔH/(TΔV).

(b) For vaporisation, assume (i) the liquid's molar volume is negligible beside the vapour's, so ΔV ≈ V^v, and (ii) the vapour is an ideal gas, V^v = RT/P. Then dP/dT = PΔH/(RT²), or d ln P/dT = ΔH/(RT²). Assuming (iii) ΔH is constant over the range and integrating: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

(c) 1/363.15 − 1/373.15 = 7.379 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Then ln(P₂/1.013) = −(40 660/8.314) × 7.379 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ −0.361, so P₂ = 1.013 × e^(−0.361) ≈ 0.706 bar. This is within about 0.6% of the tabulated 0.702 bar. The agreement is good because the 10 K range is small, so ΔH hardly changes, and at about 1 bar water vapour is close to ideal.

(d) ΔH = R ln(P₂/P₁)/(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) = 8.314 × ln(1.014/0.474)/(1/353.15 − 1/373.15) = 8.314 × 0.7606/(1.518 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 41.7 kJ/mol. This is about 2.5% above 40.66 kJ/mol, which is the value at 100 °C. The latent heat of water increases as temperature falls, so the average over 80–100 °C is larger. The fitted value also absorbs the small errors from treating the vapour as ideal and neglecting the liquid's volume.

(e) dP/dT = ΔH_fus/(TΔV) = 6010/(273.15 × (−1.63 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ −1.35 × 10⁷ Pa/K, or about −135 bar/K. The slope is negative because water contracts on melting (ice is less dense than liquid water). Increasing the pressure therefore lowers the melting point, but only by about 0.0074 K per bar, so very large pressures are needed to have a noticeable effect.
